Et tu, Brute? The famous phrase "Et tu, Brute?"—And you, Brutus?—is attributed to Julius Caesar upon recognizing his ally Marcus Brutus among his assassins. However, there is no historical evidence Caesar actually said this. William Shakespeare invented the line for his 1599 play Julius Caesar, and it has since become the canonical final words, conflating Shakespeare's theatrical fiction with historical fact.

The Latin phrase does not appear in any contemporary historical account of Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE. It is entirely Shakespeare's invention for dramatic effect. Marcus Brutus was indeed a respected senator and a friend of Caesar, and he was part of the conspiracy against him. His betrayal is central to the tragedy.

Shakespeare placed the phrase in Act III, Scene 2 of Julius Caesar to add pathos. Caesar's shock at Brutus's involvement amplifies his tragic downfall. Popular culture has adopted the phrase as historical fact, with countless references treating it as a genuine quotation from Caesar's final moments.

The conspiracy against Caesar was driven by senators' fears of his accumulating power and desire to restore the Republic, not personal animosity from Brutus alone. The assassination itself occurred on the Ides of March, March fifteenth, and Caesar was stabbed by multiple senators, including Brutus.
